# Connective tissue

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Rheumatology and immunology > Basics of rheumatology > Connective tissue*

[Original Article Link](/library/ro0fWS)

---

## Summary

Connective tissue is the most abundant type of tissue in the body. It serves to connect and support other tissues and also has regulatory and immunologic functions. Connective tissue consists of cells, mainly <u>fibroblasts</u>, and an <u>extracellular matrix</u> (<u>ECM</u>). The specific composition of the <u>ECM</u> determines the biochemical properties of the connective tissue. There are many different types of connective tissue, with loose and <u>dense connective tissue</u> being the most common.




Disorders of connective tissue are discussed in “<u>Connective tissue diseases</u>”

## Cells of the connective tissue

### Resident cells




* Fibroblasts (the most common cell type in connective tissue)

* Origin: derived from <u>mesenchymal stem cells</u>

* Function: synthesis and organization of the <u>ECM</u>

* Histological features: spindle-shaped cells arranged in a branching pattern

* Fibrocytes: a <u>fibroblast</u> with low metabolic activity

* Myofibroblasts: contractile hybrid cells with features of both <u>fibroblasts</u> and <u>smooth muscle cells</u>

* Function: synthesize <u>ECM</u> components and are involved in the proliferative <u>phase of wound healing</u>

* Histological features: indistinguishable from <u>fibroblasts</u> under the <u>light microscope</u> without <u>immunohistochemical</u> staining for, e.g., <u>actin</u> or <u>desmin</u>

* <u>Chondroblasts</u> and <u>chondrocytes</u>

* Function: produce and maintain the <u>ECM</u> in <u>cartilage</u>

* See “<u>Cartilage</u>.”





### Transient <u>immune cells</u>



* <u>Immune cells</u>: <u>lymphocytes</u>, <u>plasma cells</u>, <u>macrophages</u>, and <u>mast cells</u>

---

## Extracellular matrix

The <u>extracellular matrix</u> (<u>ECM</u>) is composed of various macromolecules arranged in a three-dimensional structure. Its specific composition determines the biochemical properties of the connective tissue.




### <u>Extracellular matrix fibers</u> (<u>connective tissue fibers</u>)




<u>Collagen</u> molecules are the basis of <u>collagen fibers</u> and <u>reticular fibers</u>. They account for the majority of <u>proteins</u> in the <u>ECM</u>, which makes them the most abundant <u>proteins</u> in the human body. <u>Elastic fibers</u> are composed of <u>elastin</u> molecules and can be found together with <u>collagen fibers</u> in tissues that require elasticity in addition to tensile strength, e.g., the <u>lung</u>.




| Overview of extracellular matrix fibers |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | Collagen fibers | Reticular fibers | Elastic fibers |
| Main molecule | <br>* <u>Collagen</u> molecules (especially <u>type I collagen</u>)<br><br> | <br>* <u>Collagen</u> molecules (especially <u>type III collagen</u>)<br><br> | <br>* <u>Elastin</u> molecules<br><br> |
| Characteristics | <br>* Tensile strength<br><br> | <br>* Tensile strength with limited elasticity<br><br> | <br>* Elasticity<br><br> |
| Occurrence | <br><br>* <u>Dense connective tissue</u><br><br>* <u>Loose connective tissue</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Reticular connective tissue</u><br><br>* <u>Basement membrane</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Tissues that require high elasticity and the ability to recoil after a transient stretch (e.g., aorta, <u>lungs</u>, <u>skin</u>, <u>vocal folds</u>, <u>ligamenta flava</u>)<br><br> |
| Associated <u>proteins</u> | <br>* –<br><br> | <br>* –<br><br> | <br><br>* Fibrillin<br><br>* Fibulin-5<br><br><br> |





> [!NOTE]
> <u>Marfan syndrome</u> is caused by a mutation in the <u>fibrillin</u> <u>gene</u> (<u>FBN1</u>).

#### Collagen




* Definition

* A family of glycoproteins synthesized by <u>fibroblasts</u> and secreted (as triple-stranded <u>procollagen</u>) into the <u>extracellular space</u>

* <u>Collagen</u> is the most ubiquitous and abundant protein in humans.

* Structure: A <u>collagen</u> molecule is a protein with a repeating <u>amino acid</u> sequence (Gly-X-Y)<sub>n</sub>.

* The first <u>amino acid</u> of this triplet is <u>glycine</u> (<u>collagen</u> is comprised of ⅓ <u>glycine</u>).

* Position X: most commonly <u>proline</u>;  (also common: <u>lysine</u>, <u>hydroxylysine</u>)

* Position Y: most commonly <u>hydroxyproline</u>;  (also common: <u>hydroxylysine</u>, <u>lysine</u>)

* Function: organize, strengthen, and provide elasticity to the <u>extracellular matrix</u>

* Types

* Of the 42 <u>genes</u> coding for <u>collagen</u> chains, 28 types of <u>collagen</u> triple helices can be assembled. [[1]](/library/Unbbs8)

* Some <u>collagen types</u> (e.g., <u>collagen</u> type I, II, III, V, XI) form fibrils while others do not (e.g., <u>collagen</u> type IV, VIII, X).





| Types of collagen |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | Tissue distribution | Related conditions |
| <br>Type I collagen (90% of body <u>collagen</u>) | <br>* Bone (produced by <u>osteoblasts</u>), <u>skin</u>, <u>tendons</u>, <u>ligaments</u>, <u>fascia</u>, <u>dentin</u>, <u>cornea</u>, internal organs, <u>scar</u> tissue (late stages of <u>wound healing</u>)<br><br> | <br>* <u>Osteogenesis imperfecta</u> type I: decreased production<br><br> |
| Type II collagen | <br>* <u>Cartilage</u> (including <u>hyaline</u>), <u>vitreous humor</u> of the <u>eye</u>, <u>intervertebral discs</u> (<u>nucleus pulposus</u>)<br><br> | <br>* Achondrogenesis (type II) [[2]](/library/O3YIiK)<br><br> |
| Type III collagen (<u>reticulin</u>) | <br>* <u>Reticular fibers</u> in <u>skin</u>, <u>blood vessels</u>, <u>granulation tissue</u>, <u>uterus</u>, <u>scar</u> tissue (early stages of <u>wound healing</u>), fetal tissue in early embryos and throughout <u>embryogenesis</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Ehlers-Danlos syndrome</u> (vascular type): decreased production [[3]](/library/l3YviK)<br><br> |
| Type IV collagen | <br>* <u>Basement membranes</u>, <u>lens</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Alport syndrome</u>: decreased production<br><br>* <u>Goodpasture syndrome</u>: <u>autoantibodies</u> target <u>type IV collagen</u><br><br><br> |
| Type V collagen | <br>* Bone, <u>skin</u>, fetal tissue, <u>placenta</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Ehlers-Danlos syndrome</u> (classic type)<br><br> |





* Degradation: enzymatic via specific collagenases (<u>zinc</u>-dependent proteinases that belong to the <u>matrix metalloproteinases</u> family)

* Synthesis: Collagens are synthesized at the <u>rough ER</u> (<u>rER</u>) and undergo extensive post-translational modifications.





| <br>Overview of collagen synthesis <br> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Stages | Process | Site | <br>Intermediate product (precursors of <u>collagen</u>) |
| 1. <u>Translation</u> | <br><br>* Synthesis of <u>polypeptide</u> chain (pro-<u>α chain</u> with repeating Gly-X-Y sequence) and further processing<br><br>* While the amount of <u>glycine</u> in <u>collagen</u> is quite stable (⅓ of <u>collagen</u>), the amount of <u>lysine</u> and <u>proline</u> is more variable.<br><br><br> | <br>* IC (<u>rER</u>)<br><br> | <br>* Preprocollagen<br><br> |
| 2. <u>Hydroxylation</u> | <br><br>* <u>Hydroxylation</u> of <u>proline</u> residue to hydroxyproline<br><br>* <u>Hydroxylation</u> of <u>lysine</u> residue to hydroxylysine at the X and Y positions of the <u>collagen</u> <u>peptide</u> chain<br><br>* Enzymes: prolyl hydroxylase and lysyl hydroxylase: <u>vitamin C</u>-dependent hydroxylases (additional <u>cofactors</u> are <u>α-ketoglutarate</u>, Fe<sup>2+</sup>, and O<sub>2</sub>)<br><br>* Function: prerequisite for the formation of stable triple helices<br><br>* Laboratory quantification of <u>collagen</u> is performed via measurement of <u>hydroxyproline</u>.<br><br><br> | <br>* IC (<u>rER</u>)<br><br> | <br>* Pro-<u>α chain</u><br><br> |
| 3. <u>Glycosylation</u> | <br><br>* <u>Glycosylation</u> of pro-<u>α chain</u>: enzymatic binding of <u>carbohydrate</u> to <u>hydroxylysine</u> via hydrogen and <u>disulfide bonds</u><br><br>* Function: labeling of <u>proteins</u> for exocytosis<br><br><br> | <br>* IC (<u>rER</u>)<br><br> |  |
| 4. Formation of a triple helix | <br><br>* Formation of <u>disulfide bonds</u> and <u>hydrogen bonds</u> between three α-chains to form a triple helix<br><br>* Function: requirement for fibril formation (fibrillogenesis)<br><br><br> | <br>* IC (<u>rER</u>)<br><br> | <br>* Procollagen (triple helix)<br><br> |
| 5. Exocytosis | <br>* Exocytosis of the <u>collagen</u> triple helix into the <u>extracellular space</u><br><br> | <br>* IC → EC<br><br> |  |
| <br>6. Proteolytic processing<br> | <br><br>* Cleavage of the <u>procollagen</u> at the disulfide-rich C terminus and N terminus regions<br><br>* Function: <u>Collagen</u> molecules become insoluble in water.<br><br><br> | <br>* EC<br><br> | <br>* Tropocollagen<br><br> |
| 7. Fibrillogenesis (cross-linking) | <br>* Formation of <u>collagen fibrils</u>: covalent cross-linking of <u>lysine</u>-<u>hydroxylysine</u> residues in adjacent tropocollagens <br><br>* Enzyme: <u>copper</u>-dependent lysyl oxidase<br><br>* Function: reinforcement of <u>tropocollagen</u> molecules<br><br> | <br>* EC<br><br> | <br>* Collagen fibrils<br><br> |
| 8. Formation of fibers | <br>* Several <u>collagen fibrils</u> accumulate to form a thick bundle (fiber)<br><br> | <br>* EC<br><br> | <br>* <u>Collagen fiber</u> (end product)<br><br> |
| Abbreviations: IC = intracellular; EC = extracellular; <u>ECM</u> =extracellular matrix; <u>rER</u> =<u>rough endoplasmic reticulum</u><br> |  |  |  |





> [!NOTE]
> Type ONE <u>collagen</u> is in bONE.
> Type TWO <u>collagen</u>: carTWOlage
> Type THREE <u>collagen</u> is deficient in the vascular type of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (3D = ThreE D).
> Type FOUR <u>collagen</u> is under the FLOOR (part of <u>basement membrane</u>).




> [!NOTE]
> <u>Vitamin C deficiency</u> leads to <u>scurvy</u> because it impairs <u>hydroxylation</u> of <u>procollagen</u> chains.




> [!NOTE]
> Impaired triple helix formation during <u>collagen synthesis</u> is the pathophysiological mechanism of <u>osteogenesis imperfecta</u>.




> [!NOTE]
> <u>Ehlers-Danlos syndrome</u> is caused by defective cleavage of <u>procollagen</u> molecules.




> [!NOTE]
> <u>Menkes disease</u> occurs as a result of defective cross-linking of <u>tropocollagen</u>.

#### Elastin




* Definition: : an elastic protein that is a major component of <u>elastic fibers</u>

* Characteristics

* Rich in the nonhydroxylated <u>amino acids</u> <u>glycine</u>, <u>proline</u>, and <u>lysine</u>, in contrast with the <u>hydroxylated proline</u> and <u>lysine</u> residues (<u>hydroxyproline</u>, <u>hydroxylysine</u>) present in <u>collagen</u>.

* Provides tissue with elasticity (via alternating <u>α-helices</u> and hydrophobic domains)

* <u>Elastin</u> has a spontaneous, disorganized spatial structure (relaxed conformation) that temporarily adopts an orderly arrangement only when stretched.

* Occurrence: tissues requiring high elasticity and the ability to recoil after a transient stretch

* Large <u>arteries</u> (e.g., aorta)

* <u>Lungs</u>

* <u>Skin</u>

* <u>Vocal folds</u>

* <u>Elastic ligaments</u> (e.g., the <u>ligamenta flava</u>, which connect the <u>vertebrae</u> and can adopt both relaxed and stretched conformations).

* Synthesis: Several <u>elastin</u> molecules are crosslinked (polymerization) and form bundles as <u>elastic fibers</u>.

* <u>Fibrillin</u> forms the scaffold for laying down tropoelastin.

* Desmosine, a pyridinium ring formed by the condensation of four <u>lysine</u> residues, forms the crosslink between <u>tropoelastin</u> molecules.

* Cross-linking between <u>tropoelastin</u> occurs extracellularly

* Formed with the aid of <u>transglutaminase</u> and <u>lysyl oxidase</u>.

* Degradation: enzymatically via <u>elastase</u> (<u>elastase</u> inhibition by <u>α<sub>1</sub>-antitrypsin</u>)





> [!NOTE]
> Defective <u>α1-antitrypsin</u> leads to increased <u>elastase</u> activity, resulting in the <u>autosomal</u> <u>codominant</u> disorder <u>α1-antitrypsin deficiency</u>, which is characterized by <u>panacinar emphysema</u> and <u>cirrhosis</u>.




> [!NOTE]
> Normal <u>aging</u> involves decreased levels of <u>dermal</u> <u>collagen</u> and <u>elastin</u> as well as decreased synthesis of <u>collagen fibrils</u>. Crosslinking is not affected by <u>aging</u>.




### Glycosaminoglycans (<u>GAGs</u>)




* Definition: a family of unbranched <u>polysaccharide</u> chains of repeating <u>disaccharide</u> units with multiple negative charges that constitute a large volume fraction of the <u>ECM</u>

* Structure: polymer of repeating <u>disaccharide</u> units

* First sugar: derivative of uronic acid (e.g., <u>glucuronic acid</u>)

* Second sugar: hexosamine (e.g., the amino sugar N-acetylglucosamine)

* Four main groups 

* Hyaluronic acid

* Chondroitin sulfate and dermatan sulfate

* Heparan sulfate

* Keratan sulfate

* Function

* Bind H<sub>2</sub>O in connective tissue due to its negative charges: act as a cushion

* Component of <u>proteoglycans</u>





### Proteoglycans




* Definition: <u>proteins</u> with numerous covalently linked <u>GAG</u> side chains

* Function

* Bind H<sub>2</sub>O → <u>shock</u> absorption and a supportive function (e.g., in <u>cartilage</u> → resistance to compression of <u>articular cartilage</u>)

* Formation of <u>cell-cell junction</u> or cell-matrix junction

* Further signaling and regulatory functions (e.g., by binding signaling molecules)

* Examples

* Aggrecan: large <u>proteoglycan</u> found in <u>cartilage</u> as an aggregate with <u>hyaluronic acid</u> → <u>shock</u> absorption withstands compression

* Decorin: small <u>proteoglycan</u> that binds <u>collagen</u> fibrils → regulates fibril assembly





![Aggrecan](media/t3wav7jusdnv0qmgw3shwr2i.jpg)

Aggrecan




### Glycoproteins of the <u>ECM</u>




* Definition: <u>proteins</u> with short <u>carbohydrate</u> side chains that contribute to the organization of the <u>extracellular matrix</u> by offering specific binding sites for cells and other matrix molecules

* Examples

* Fibronectin

* Glycoprotein important for cell-matrix interactions

* Function: binds to <u>collagen</u> and <u>integrins</u> and plays an important role in <u>embryogenesis</u> (regulates cell migration) and <u>hemostasis</u> (cross-linking of <u>fibrin</u> molecules with <u>thrombocytes</u> and <u>fibroblasts</u>)

* Laminin

* Major component and organizer of the <u>basal lamina</u> (besides <u>type IV collagen</u>)

* Function: binds to collagens, <u>integrins</u>, and <u>proteoglycans</u>





> [!NOTE]
> Proteoglycans are primarily composed of <u>carbohydrates</u> that are attached to the side of a small core protein. In contrast, glyco<u>proteins</u> are mainly composed of a protein that is attached to the side chain of a short <u>carbohydrate</u>.

## Connective tissue types

| Types of connective tissue |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Type | <br>Main components<br> | Function | Occurrence |
| <br>Loose connective tissue <br> | <br><br>* <u>Collagen fibers</u> (especially types I and III)<br><br>* <u>Elastic fibers</u><br><br>* <u>Hyaluronic acid</u><br><br>* <u>Decorin</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Structural framework for organs (interstitium)<br><br>* Attaches <u>epithelia</u> to underlying tissue<br><br>* Allows for independent movement<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Interstitium</u><br><br>* Most abundant form of connective tissue<br><br><br> |
| <br>Dense connective tissue <br> | <br>* <u>Collagen fibers</u> (especially type I)<br><br> | <br>* Provide tensile strength, especially in tissue under mechanical <u>stress</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Dense regular connective tissue : <u>tendons</u>, <u>ligaments</u>, <u>aponeurosis</u><br><br>* Dense irregular connective tissue:  <u>dermis</u> (stratum reticulare), <u>fascia</u>, <u>dura mater</u>, <u>sclera</u>, <u>cornea</u>, and organ and <u>joint capsules</u><br><br><br> |
| <br>Reticular connective tissue <br> | <br><br>* <u>Reticular fibers</u><br><br>* <u>Fibronectin</u><br><br>* Fibroblastic reticular cells<br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Reticular cells</u> and <u>reticular fibers</u> form a network, where <u>stem cells</u> from blood and the <u>immune system</u> mature.<br><br> | <br>* <u>Bone marrow</u> and <u>secondary lymphoid organs</u><br><br> |
| Elastic ligaments | <br>* <u>Elastic fibers</u> > collagenous fibers<br><br> | <br>* Provides <u>ligaments</u> with a high level of elasticity<br><br> | <br>* Yellow <u>ligament</u> (<u>ligamentum flavum</u>), <u>nuchal ligament</u><br><br> |
| Mucous connective tissue | <br>* Fine <u>collagen fibers</u>, <u>hyaluronic acid</u>, and H<sub>2</sub>O form <u>Wharton jelly</u><br><br> | <br>* Protects and insulates <u>umbilical cord</u> vessels<br><br> | <br>* <u>Umbilical cord</u><br><br> |
| Stroma of ovary | <br><br>* Few <u>reticular fibers</u><br><br>* Numerous spindle-shaped cells<br><br><br> | <br>* Follicle formation in the <u>ovary</u> (<u>folliculogenesis</u>)<br><br> | <br>* <u>Ovaries</u><br><br> |
| Specialized connective tissue | <br>* Several tissue types in the body are primarily composed of connective tissue with a specialized <u>ECM</u>.<br><br> | <br>* For further information on their special functions, please refer to the individual articles<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Ligaments</u><br><br>* <u>Tendons</u><br><br>* <u>Fascia</u><br><br>* <u>Cartilage</u><br><br>* <u>Bone tissue</u><br><br><br> |

## Clinical significance

* Fibrosis: the <u>proliferation</u> of <u>fibroblasts</u> and deposition of <u>collagen</u> in tissues

* Can be a result of a reparative process (e.g., following injury, inflammation, and/or <u>necrosis</u>): e.g., <u>cirrhosis</u>, <u>retroperitoneal fibrosis</u>
OR

* Can be a result of a reaction to chronic irritants (e.g., <u>pneumoconiosis</u>, chronic <u>lymphedema</u>)

* <u>Marfan syndrome</u>

* <u>Ehlers-Danlos syndrome</u>

* <u>Menkes disease</u>

* <u>Osteogenesis imperfecta</u>

* <u>Scurvy</u>

* <u>Connective tissue diseases</u>

* <u>Wound healing</u>

* <u>Fibroma</u>
